title: TJ Dana 30 — Stock Rating and Upgrade Options

citations.title: The Jeep Dana 30 — The Ranger Station
Dana 30, Dana 35, and Dana 44 factory specifications

summary: The TJ Dana 30 will live behind 33s with stock shafts and behind 35s if you upgrade to chromoly shafts and stronger U-joints — but the moment you add a front locker, the weak link shifts to the axle shafts and ball joints.
description:
Every TJ except the Rubicon left the factory with a front Dana 30. It's a low-pinion, 7.125" ring gear axle rated for roughly 3,500 lb gross axle weight. The ring and pinion is honestly underrated — most failures happen at the axle shafts and U-joints first, not the gears. That said, the Dana 30 has well-understood limits and an equally well-understood upgrade path.

Stock 27-spline shafts and the small 260X U-joints are reliable behind 31s and 33s with no locker. Once you bolt on 35s, the leverage at the tire patch starts to outpace what the small U-joints can handle, especially with throttle stabs in low range. Add a locker, and a stock shaft on the locked side becomes the sacrificial part — the locker eliminates the differential's natural torque relief, so any tire grip spike loads the shaft directly. Plan the upgrades in this order: U-joints, shafts, then locker.

The most common shaft upgrade is Yukon or RCV chromoly 27-spline axle shafts paired with Spicer 5-297X U-joints. The 5-297X is about 30% stronger than the stock 260X and uses larger trunnions. RCV CV-style shafts cost more (~$1,400/pair) but eliminate U-joint binding at full steering lock, which matters if you're rock crawling. Some builders go to 30-spline shafts, but the Dana 30 outer stub is still 27-spline, so the inner upgrade alone doesn't fully resolve the weak point and 30-spline shafts are harder to source in a hurry on the trail.

Ball joints are the other Dana 30 conversation. The factory ball joints have a known short service life — many TJs need replacement by 80–100k miles, sooner if the rig has been lifted. Aggressive lift angles, larger tires, and rough trails accelerate wear. Synergy, Spicer Performance, and Dynatrac all make heavy-duty replacements that last meaningfully longer.

For builds aiming above 35s with a locker, the conversation shifts to a Dana 44 front swap (junkyard XJ or Rubicon JK donor) rather than continuing to upgrade the Dana 30 — at that point, you've spent enough on the Dana 30 that the swap is the better dollar.
steps: Inspect ball joints first — grab the top of the tire at 12 and 6 o'clock and rock it; any play means replacement.
Pull both front axle shafts. Inspect U-joints for play, rust, and pitting.
If shafts are stock 27-spline with small U-joints and you run 33s+, plan a chromoly shaft + 5-297X upgrade.
Press out old ball joints with a ball joint press. Install heavy-duty replacements per torque spec (upper 80 ft-lb, lower 100 ft-lb).
Reassemble shafts with new U-joints, torque axle nut to 175 ft-lb.
If installing a locker, this is the time — pull the third member, swap the carrier, set backlash and pinion preload.
Refill diff with 75W-90 gear oil (2.0 qt) and a friction modifier if running a clutch-style limited slip.
pros: Cheaper than a full Dana 44 swap
Bolt-in upgrade path — no fabrication
Chromoly shafts and HD ball joints solve 80% of failures
Strong enough for 35s with the right shafts
cons: Locker plus stock shafts is a recipe for trail breakage
Ball joints are a known weak spot, especially lifted
30-spline upgrade is incomplete unless outers also upgrade
Above 35s, the math favors a Dana 44 swap instead

title: Front Brake Pad and Rotor Replacement

parts.name: Powerstop Z36 Truck and Tow front kit

citations.title: TJ Wrangler Front Caliper Bolt Torque Spec (11-13 ft-lb)
TJ Brake Caliper Mounting Torque Discussion

summary: TJ front pads run 30,000–45,000 miles depending on terrain and gear. The 1997–2002 TJ uses a 3/8" hex bit on the caliper slider; the 2003+ Rubicon and LJ use a slightly larger bolt head. Caliper slider torque is 11–13 ft-lb — easy to strip.
description:
The TJ front brake setup is single-piston floating caliper on vented rotors, same general layout as the XJ Cherokee it shares an axle with. Two slider pins hold the caliper; two large bracket bolts hold the bracket to the steering knuckle. What makes the TJ slightly different from the XJ is the slider bolts use a 3/8" hex (Allen) head on 1997–2002 trucks — you'll need a hex bit socket, not a regular hex socket, to break them loose without rounding them.

A note on tools: many TJ owners discover mid-job that their breaker bar set is missing the 3/8" hex bit. Pick one up before starting. The slider bolts often blue-Loctite from the factory and don't always come loose easily — a quality bit and a breaker bar beat a stripped slider every time.

Pad recommendations for the TJ skew toward heavier compounds than the XJ because TJs are typically lifted on bigger tires more aggressively. Stock pads from Mopar (PN 5018572AB) are fine for a stock-tire Sport. Anything past 33s, add weight, or tow occasionally — go to Powerstop Z36 or EBC Yellowstuff. The TJ's brake system is the same hardware as a much lighter vehicle; the only way to make it deal with 35s and a winch bumper is harder pad compound and a heavier rotor.

Rotor choice: Centric Premium ($40 each) or Powerstop Evolution ($45 each) are solid stock-replacement options that often outlast OEM. Skip the cheap blank rotors from chain auto parts stores — they warp within 5,000 miles on a daily-driven TJ. Mopar OEM rotors are decent but expensive; Centric Premium gives 90% of the durability for half the price.

The TJ caliper slider bolts are the most-stripped bolts on the front end. Chrysler spec is 11–13 ft-lb. That feels finger-tight to anyone used to lug nuts. Use a torque wrench. Over-torque and you either snap the bolt or strip the bracket threads — both leave you with a non-driveable Jeep until you helicoil the bracket or find a new one.
steps: Crack lug nuts (19mm), lift the front of the TJ, support on stands at the front axle.
Remove front wheels. Pull the master cylinder reservoir cap and drape a rag.
Remove the two caliper slider bolts using a 3/8" hex bit (1997–2002) or 13mm socket (2003+ LJ/Rubicon).
Slide caliper off the bracket. Hang from a wire — don't let it dangle by the hose.
Compress the caliper piston back with a C-clamp using an old pad as a buffer.
Pull the old pads from the bracket. Note clip orientation.
To replace rotors: remove the two bracket bolts (15mm on early TJ, 18mm on Rubicon/LJ) from the steering knuckle. Lift bracket off. Pull old rotor.
Wire-brush the hub mating face. Rust ridges here cause runout.
Install new rotor (light anti-seize on the hub face only, not on the friction surface). Reinstall bracket and torque to 100 ft-lb.
Install new pads with new anti-rattle clips. Light brake grease on pad backs and slider pins.
Slide caliper over pads onto the bracket. Reinstall slider bolts and torque to 11 ft-lb — do not exceed.
Reinstall wheels, torque lugs to 100 ft-lb.
Pump brake pedal until firm. Top off reservoir.
Bed in pads: 8–10 moderate stops from 35 mph, then 2–3 harder stops from 50 mph.
pros: Shared parts with XJ Cherokee — wide aftermarket support
Common floating caliper, no special tools beyond hex bit
Centric Premium rotors outlast OEM at half the price
Stock pad life 30K–45K on daily-driven TJ
cons: Caliper slider bolts (11 ft-lb) easily over-torqued and stripped
3/8" hex bit required for 1997–2002 sliders — easy to miss when prepping
Stock brakes undersized for lifted 33"+ builds; need harder pad compound
Bargain rotors warp in 5,000 miles — buy Centric or better

title: AX-15 Manual Transmission Service

citations.title: AX-15 Manual Transmission Service — JeepSpecs
Wrangler TJ Fluid Capacities
TJ Transmission and Transfer Case Fluid Change

summary: Drain and refill the AX-15 with 3.3 quarts of 75W-90 GL-4 (not GL-5) every 30,000 miles — 60-minute job, magnetic drain plug, no special tools.
description:
The AX-15 is a 5-speed Aisin manual that came in TJs from 1997 to 2004 paired with the 4.0L. It's the strongest manual Jeep ever bolted behind the 4.0 and it shifts cleanly for decades when the fluid is fresh. What kills an AX-15 early is the wrong fluid — and there is a persistent forum debate about what "the right fluid" actually is. The factory service manual specifies GL-3, but GL-3 is essentially extinct in the consumer market. The Mopar PN for the original fluid (75W-90 GL-3) has been superseded.

The honest answer: run 75W-90 GL-4. GL-5 gear oils contain sulfur-phosphorus additives that attack the AX-15's yellow-metal synchronizer parts and will cause crunchy shifts within a few thousand miles. Redline MT-90 (75W-90 GL-4) is the most-recommended choice on TJ forums for a reason — it shifts smoothly cold and hot. Pennzoil Synchromesh is the other widely-used option, especially for owners who want a slightly thinner feel in cold weather. Stay away from anything labeled "gear oil 80W-90" off the auto parts shelf unless you confirm the GL-4 rating on the bottle.

Capacity is 3.3 quarts (some sources round to 3.25). The drain plug is on the passenger-side bottom of the case and takes a 15/16" or 24mm socket. It's magnetic — pull it after every change and wipe the metal paste off. Fine glitter is normal. Chunks, shavings, or anything the size of a grain of rice means a synchro or bearing is on its way out and you should pull the transmission for inspection.

Crack the fill plug FIRST before opening the drain. The fill plug is on the driver's side of the case (square 3/8" or 1/2" drive). If the fill plug is seized and you've already drained, you have no way to refill without removing the transmission.

While you're under there: feel the shift rail boot at the top of the transmission for cracks (a torn boot lets water into the case), inspect the rear yoke seal for weeping, and check the slave cylinder line for swelling if you have a hydraulic clutch.
steps: Drive the Jeep 10–15 miles to warm the gear oil. Park on level ground.
Locate the fill plug on the driver's side of the case. Break it loose first — do not skip this step.
Position drain pan under the passenger-side drain plug. Remove the drain plug with a 15/16" or 24mm socket.
Let it drain fully — 15 to 20 minutes for warm fluid.
Wipe the magnetic drain plug clean. Inspect the magnet for chunks or large shavings. Reinstall and torque to 14–20 ft-lbs.
Use a fluid pump to refill through the fill hole until fluid drips back out — about 3.3 quarts.
Reinstall the fill plug and torque to 25 ft-lbs.
Drive a few miles, run through all five gears plus reverse, and recheck for leaks at the drain and fill plugs.
pros: One-hour job with a $40 fluid bill
Catches early bearing or synchro failure via drain plug debris
Restores notchy-cold shifts that the original fluid no longer handles
cons: Wrong fluid (GL-5) will damage the synchros — easy mistake at the parts counter
Fill plug seizes on rust-belt TJs and can require heat to break free
Capacity is awkward to measure — fill until it overflows, not by quart count

title: Front Driveshaft — CV Joint Replacement

parts.name: Spicer 211179X CV centering yoke + spring kit (TJ Rubicon)
Tom Wood's custom CV front driveshaft (TJ Rubicon, 1330)
Denny's rebuild kit — TJ Rubicon 1330 CV (2 u-joints + centering yoke)

citations.title: Denny's TJ Rubicon 1330 CV Rebuild Kit
WranglerTJ Forum — Driveshaft torque specs
Quadratec — Wrangler TJ Driveshaft Parts

summary: A vibrating front driveshaft on a TJ is almost always a worn u-joint or, on Rubicons, a collapsed CV centering yoke — both are rebuildable for under $200, but past 4" of lift most TJs are better off with a new CV-style shaft.
description:
Non-Rubicon TJs (1997–2002 and 2003–2006 non-Rubi) came with a plain two-u-joint front driveshaft. It's a 1310-series shaft, cheap to service, and tolerant of small lifts. Rubicons got a 1330-series shaft with a CV (double-cardan) joint at the transfer case end — this lets the driveline run at steeper angles without vibration, which matters once you lift the truck or run a Slip Yoke Eliminator on the rear. The CV joint has two u-joints back-to-back plus a centering ball and spring inside the yoke. That centering ball is the wear part most people miss.

Symptoms of a worn u-joint: a vibration that comes in at a specific speed range (usually 40–60 mph), a clunk on shift into 4WD, or visible rust dust at the cap edges. Symptoms of a collapsed centering yoke on a CV shaft: vibration at low speed and under load that doesn't track with engine RPM, and obvious play when you grab the shaft and rock it side-to-side at the t-case yoke. Don't replace just one u-joint on a CV shaft — do both u-joints and the centering yoke together. Once one is worn, the other isn't far behind, and the labor is identical.

Plan the job around removing the shaft. The four straps on the axle pinion yoke and four bolts on the t-case flange come off with the shaft mostly in place. Mark the orientation of the shaft to both yokes before you pull it — re-installing 180° out can introduce a vibration. Once on the bench, knock out the old u-joint caps with a socket and a vise (a u-joint press is faster), clean the yoke ears, and seat the new caps evenly. The CV centering yoke press-fits with a new spring; follow Denny's or Spicer's kit instructions on spring orientation.

If your TJ is sitting on 4" or more of lift and a CV-style shaft isn't already there, the rebuild is a band-aid. A Tom Wood's custom CV front shaft drops in, ends the vibration permanently, and is built for the operating angle your suspension actually runs. $500-ish complete is cheaper than re-doing u-joints every two years on a non-CV shaft that's living past its design angle.
steps: Lift the front of the truck, support on stands, place transmission in neutral.
Mark the orientation of the shaft to both the axle pinion yoke and t-case flange with a paint marker.
Remove the four 12mm strap bolts at the axle pinion. Catch the u-joint caps so they don't fall.
Remove the four 13mm flange bolts at the t-case end.
Pull the shaft off the truck, support the t-case yoke so it doesn't drop.
Bench-press old u-joints out of the shaft yokes.
On Rubicon CV shafts, pry the centering yoke out and replace with kit-included new yoke and spring.
Install new u-joints — caps go in evenly, snap rings seated, joint moves freely with no bind.
Grease the fittings until grease comes out all four cap seals.
Reinstall the shaft to match your alignment marks. Torque axle strap bolts to 15 ft-lbs (hand-tight on the straps), t-case flange bolts to 18–20 ft-lbs, large flange nuts to 160 ft-lbs if applicable.
pros: Rebuild is under $200 in parts
New u-joints solve most TJ vibration complaints
Greaseable Spicer u-joints last longer than sealed OE
CV shaft handles steeper lift angles
cons: A non-CV shaft at 4"+ lift will vibrate again — rebuilding is a delay, not a fix
CV centering yoke is fiddly to press without the right tools
Cheap u-joints fail fast — buy Spicer or Neapco, not no-name

title: NP231 Transfer Case — Service and Weak Points

citations.title: NP231 fluid type — Wrangler Forum
JB Conversions NP231 SYE
Teraflex SYE install — Quadratec

summary: The NP231 in your TJ is one of the toughest chain-driven transfer cases ever built — the gears almost never fail, but the slip-yoke output is its one real weakness and lifted Jeeps need a slip-yoke eliminator.
description:
The NP231 (also called NP231J) is the transfer case bolted to nearly every TJ except the Rubicon. The planetary low range, drive sprockets, and chain are overbuilt — owners routinely run them past 200,000 miles with nothing but fluid changes. The original 27-spline rear output shaft is the one weak point, and the slip-yoke design at the rear output is the design choice that bites lifted Jeeps. Maintenance is short and cheap. The slip-yoke conversion is a decision, not a repair, and it matters once you go past 3 inches of lift.

For fluid service, the NP231 holds roughly 2.2 quarts of ATF. Mopar specifies ATF+4 and that is the right choice for warranty and longevity, but the case is genuinely not picky — Dexron, Mercon, or ATF+4 all work fine, and most TJ owners run ATF+4 because they already buy it for the transmission. Change the fluid every 30,000 miles or sooner if you wheel in water. Water in the case looks milky and is the fastest way to kill bearings.

The slip-yoke story is the part most TJ owners need to understand before they lift. The NP231 rear output is a long splined shaft that the driveshaft yoke slides onto and off of as the suspension articulates. Stock, it works. Lifted, the driveshaft angle steepens, the yoke loads off-center, and the rear output seal starts weeping. Worse, the longer effective driveshaft length means a shorter shaft, which amplifies vibration at highway speed. A slip-yoke eliminator (SYE) kit replaces the long splined output with a short fixed yoke, then pairs with a CV-style driveshaft. Once installed, the case stops leaking and the geometry tolerates 4–6 inches of lift without driveline vibration.

SYE options range from budget to professional. The Rough Country shaft kit around $130 is the cheapest path and works if you do not need a new tail housing. The Teraflex 2204000 kit around $295 swaps the output shaft and tail housing — the most common mid-tier choice. The JB Conversions Super Short SYE around $425 is the strongest available and uses a 32-spline output that handles 35s and a built motor without flinching. Pair any SYE with a new front-bolt CV driveshaft (Tom Wood's, Adams) and call it done.
steps: For fluid change: warm the case with a short drive, then position a drain pan under the transfer case.
Remove the 13mm fill plug first (top of case) to confirm it will come out, then remove the drain plug.
Let the case drain fully, then reinstall the drain plug torqued to 22 ft-lbs.
Pump fresh ATF+4 into the fill hole until it overflows. The case is level-full when fluid runs out.
Reinstall the fill plug torqued to 22 ft-lbs and wipe clean.
For SYE install: remove the rear driveshaft, support the case, drop the tail housing, swap to the SYE shaft and housing per kit instructions, refill with ATF+4.
Order a new CV-style rear driveshaft sized to the new yoke-to-pinion distance — measure with the suspension at ride height.
pros: Fluid change is 30 minutes and under $30
NP231 internals are nearly bulletproof — bearings and chain last 200k+
SYE eliminates the rear output leak and tames driveline vibration
JB and Teraflex kits both bolt on with standard hand tools
cons: Slip-yoke design weeps under lift and angle
Original 27-spline output limits power-handling on heavily built rigs
SYE plus driveshaft is $400–$700 all in
Water intrusion kills the chain bearings quickly

title: Serpentine Belt Replacement
tools_required: 1/2 breaker bar or serpentine belt tool

citations.title: Mopar Serpentine Belt 5281668AA listing
Wrangler TJ Forum — belt part number discussion

summary: If your TJ's belt is older than five years or you can see cracks across the ribs when you flex it, replace it before it strands you — total job is under an hour with one wrench.
description:
The TJ runs a single serpentine belt driving the alternator, power steering pump, water pump, A/C compressor (if equipped), and on some years the idler. A snapped belt kills charging and steering at the same time, and on the 4.0L it also kills the water pump, so an overheat is minutes away. Belts crack with age more than mileage — a garage-queen TJ with 30k on the clock and 10 years on the belt is just as likely to grenade one as a daily driver.

Part numbers depend on year and accessories. For 2000–2006 4.0L with A/C, the Mopar belt is 5281668AA. The Gates equivalent is K060910 (six-rib, ~91" effective length). For 4.0L without A/C, use a 75" six-rib (Gates K060749 or similar). For the 2.5L four-cylinder, length differs again — confirm by VIN at Gates.com or measure your old belt before buying.

The tensioner is a spring-loaded pulley on the driver's-side front of the engine. Rotate it counterclockwise with a 1/2" breaker bar or a dedicated serpentine belt tool to release tension. Slide the old belt off, route the new one according to the diagram on the radiator support (or photograph the old routing before removal — this is the single most common mistake). Let the tensioner spring back against the new belt. Done.

While the belt is off, spin every accessory pulley by hand. Any roughness, wobble, or grinding means a bearing is on the way out — tensioner, idler, or water pump are the usual suspects. Replace anything that doesn't spin clean. A fresh belt on a dying idler will tear itself up in months.
steps: Park the TJ, key off, hood up, engine cool.
Photograph the existing belt routing or note the diagram on the radiator support.
Position a 1/2" breaker bar on the tensioner pulley center bolt.
Rotate the tensioner counterclockwise to relieve tension.
Slide the belt off the alternator pulley first, then off the tensioner.
Spin each pulley by hand — alternator, idler, tensioner, water pump, P/S pump, A/C.
Route the new belt per diagram, slipping it onto every pulley except the alternator last.
Pull tensioner counterclockwise again, slip the belt onto the alternator pulley.
Release the tensioner slowly against the new belt.
Verify routing, start engine, watch for proper tracking with no squeals.
pros: Cheapest preventive job in the engine bay
30–60 minutes start to finish
No special tools beyond a breaker bar
Lets you inspect every accessory pulley while you're in there
cons: Wrong belt length is a real risk — confirm by VIN or measure the old one
Tensioner can be tight to break loose if it has never been serviced
Mis-routed belt will shred immediately on startup

title: Brake Fluid Flush

parts.name: ATE Type 200 (amber, German spec) — for DOT 4 upgrade

citations.title: TJ Forum — Brake Fluid Capacity Discussion
TJ Brake Fluid Change Procedure

summary: The TJ specs DOT 3, but DOT 4 is a smart upgrade for any rig that sees mountain descents or heavy towing. Plan on 32oz of fluid and a one-person gravity bleed or a two-person pedal bleed — both work.
description:
Brake fluid is hygroscopic, which is a fancy way of saying it sucks water out of the air. Wet fluid boils at a lower temperature than dry fluid, and the moment your fluid boils mid-pedal, you have no brakes. The factory recommends flushing every two years — almost nobody does, and almost nobody should be surprised when their pedal goes soft on a long descent down Schnebly Hill. If your fluid in the reservoir looks dark amber or coffee-colored, you're overdue.

Start by sucking the old fluid out of the master cylinder reservoir with a turkey baster. Get every drop you can without dragging the screen at the bottom. Refill with fresh fluid to the MAX line. This step alone replaces about 30% of the system's volume and is worth doing on its own if you're short on time.

For the actual flush, the TJ bleed sequence is rear passenger → rear driver → front passenger → front driver. Furthest from the master cylinder first, closest last. Pop a 10mm box wrench on the bleeder, slide a piece of clear 1/4" vinyl tubing over the nipple, and run the tubing into a bottle with about an inch of fresh fluid in the bottom (the fluid in the bottle keeps air from sucking back in).

Two-person method: helper presses the pedal slowly to the floor, you crack the bleeder, fluid pushes out, you close the bleeder, helper releases. Repeat five or six times per wheel until clear fluid runs through the tubing. Critical rule — never let the master cylinder run dry. Top it off after every wheel. A dry master cylinder pulls air into the ABS module on later TJs and turns a 90-minute job into a several-hour ordeal.

Plan on about a quart of fluid total for a proper flush. Buy two quarts so you're never tempted to skimp. If you're switching from DOT 3 to DOT 4, just flush thoroughly — they're chemically compatible. Do not mix DOT 5 (silicone) with anything; that's a full rebuild conversation.
steps: Park on level ground, wheels chocked. Open the hood.
Use a turkey baster to remove old fluid from the master cylinder reservoir.
Refill the reservoir to MAX with fresh fluid.
Crack each bleeder loose with a 10mm wrench before starting, then re-snug. (Confirms they aren't seized.)
Start at rear passenger wheel. Slide clear tubing over the bleeder nipple into a catch bottle with fresh fluid in the bottom.
Helper depresses the pedal slowly. Open the bleeder, let fluid flow, close the bleeder before pedal hits floor. Helper releases pedal.
Repeat 5–6 times per wheel until fluid running through tubing is clear and bubble-free.
Check the master cylinder after every wheel and top off — never let it run dry.
Move to rear driver, then front passenger, then front driver in that order.
Final master cylinder top-off to MAX. Press the pedal — it should be firm.
Test in driveway at low speed before hitting the road.
pros: $15 of fluid prevents brake fade on long descents
Restores firm pedal feel that owners often blame on calipers or master cylinders
One of the highest safety-to-effort ratios in DIY maintenance
cons: Letting the master cylinder run dry pulls air into the ABS module on later TJs
Brake fluid eats paint — wipe spills immediately
Two-person method is faster but you need a helper

title: Coolant System Flush and Inspection

citations.title: WranglerTJForum — cooling system flush writeup
WranglerForum — TJ 4.0 coolant capacity thread
CarCareKiosk — 2004 Wrangler 4.0L coolant flush video

summary: Drain the radiator and block, flush with distilled water until the runoff is clear, then refill with HOAT (G-05) coolant at 50/50. The TJ 4.0L holds about 2.6 gallons dry; plan for 1.5 gallons of new coolant on a drain-and-fill.
description:
The TJ 4.0L cooling system is robust, but coolant breaks down chemically every 5 years regardless of mileage. Once the corrosion inhibitors are spent, the inside of your radiator, heater core, and block start eating themselves. A fresh flush is cheap insurance and the most common cause of TJ overheating is not a bad water pump — it is a radiator core silted shut from a decade of skipped flushes.

Full dry capacity is 10.5 quarts (about 2.6 gallons). A standard drain through the radiator petcock recovers around 1.5 gallons, which is what you replace on a routine service. If the existing coolant is brown, rusty, or smells off, you need a full flush — drain the radiator, drain the block (8mm hex plug on the passenger side of the engine, just above the starter), and then run distilled water through the system until clear.

Coolant choice matters. The factory spec for 1997–2001 TJs is the green ethylene glycol coolant; 2002+ shipped with HOAT (Mopar's pink). Either is fine for older Jeeps as long as you fully flush before switching. The safe, modern answer for any TJ is Zerex G-05 — it is the OEM HOAT formula sold under the Valvoline label and is compatible with iron blocks and brass/copper radiators. Stay away from universal "works with everything" coolants; they tend to gel when mixed with leftover residue.

A few things to inspect while the system is empty: pressure-test the radiator cap (16 psi is spec), squeeze the upper and lower hoses for soft spots and cracks at the bend, and look at the back of the water pump weep hole for crusty buildup. If the thermostat is original, this is the moment to swap it for a $14 Mopar 195°F replacement and stop guessing about why the temp gauge wanders.

Refilling needs a bleed. The TJ has a high spot in the heater core circuit that traps air. With the cap off, start the engine, set the heater on full hot, and let the system burp for 10–15 minutes. Top off as the level drops. Drive a heat cycle, let it cool overnight, and check the level again before you call it done.
steps: Park on level ground, engine cold. Remove the radiator cap.
Place a drain pan under the radiator. Open the petcock (lower passenger side) — turn the wing tab counterclockwise.
Drain fully. For a complete flush, also remove the block drain plug (8mm hex, passenger side above starter).
Close the petcock and block plug. Reinstall both.
Optional full flush: refill with plain distilled water, run engine to temp with heater on, drain again. Repeat until water runs clear.
Refill the radiator with 50/50 G-05 (or premix) to the top. Fill the overflow bottle to the FULL HOT line.
Leave the cap off. Start engine, heater on full hot, idle 10–15 minutes.
Top off the radiator as the level drops while air bleeds out.
Install cap. Drive a heat cycle. Recheck level the next morning.
pros: One of the cheapest preventative jobs you can do — $35 in fluid
Catches a failing thermostat, weak cap, or soft hose before it strands you
Restores cooling capacity if the system was full of old, depleted coolant
No special tools beyond a drain pan and a garden hose
cons: Petcock on older TJs gets brittle and can break off — be gentle
Skipping the heater-on bleed traps air and causes false overheating
Mixing coolant types without a flush causes gel and corrosion
Block drain plug is in an awkward spot above the starter

title: Differential Fluid Change — Dana 30/35/44

citations.title: Wrangler TJ Forum — Fluid Capacities and Recommendations
Motobilt — Jeep Wrangler Differential Fluid Capacity Chart

summary: Change TJ differential fluid every 30,000 miles or every wet trail run — Dana 30 front takes about 1.25 quarts, Dana 35 rear takes about 1.7 quarts, Dana 44 rear takes about 2 quarts of 75W-90 synthetic gear oil.
description:
The TJ Wrangler shipped with three axle combinations: Dana 30 front on every model, Dana 35 rear on most non-Rubicon trims, and Dana 44 rear on the Rubicon (2003–2006) and some early Sahara/65th Anniversary builds. All three use the same basic service procedure — pull the cover, drain, scrape, reseal, refill through the fill plug — and all three benefit from a 75W-90 or 75W-140 synthetic gear oil. The most common mistake is changing the rear without checking what's actually back there. A Dana 35 has a smaller, more rounded cover; the Dana 44 cover is larger with a flatter bottom edge and 10 bolts.

Capacities differ. The Dana 30 front takes roughly 1.25 quarts (1.65 quarts on 1997 models, which used a slightly different housing). The Dana 35 rear takes about 1.7 quarts. The Dana 44 Rubicon rear takes 2 quarts. Buy 3 quarts if you've got the Dana 30 + Dana 35 combination, 4 quarts if you've got the Dana 30 + Dana 44 combination, and you'll have enough to refill both with a little left over for spillage.

Fluid choice matters more than the brand. 75W-90 GL-5 synthetic is the daily-driver standard. If you tow regularly or run 33s and above with regular trail use, step up to 75W-140 synthetic — the extra viscosity protects the ring and pinion under load. Skip the cheapest conventional 80W-90 unless you're flushing fluid every 15k miles. Rubicon Tru-Lok lockers do not require friction modifier. Trac-Lok limited-slip differentials (often found in the Dana 44 rear, some Dana 35s) require 4 oz of Mopar friction modifier (P/N 4318060AB) per fill, or the clutches will chatter on turns.

Most TJ axles do not have a drain plug. You drain by removing the rear differential cover, which means you'll also be replacing or reusing the cover gasket. RTV silicone (Permatex Ultra Black) is the OEM-style seal — clean both surfaces fully, lay a 3/16" bead around the bolt circle, install the cover, and let RTV cure 30 minutes before refilling. A Lubelocker reusable gasket is the upgrade — install dry, no cure time, and reusable for the next service.
steps: Drive the vehicle for 10 minutes to warm the fluid for easier draining. Park level.
Place a drain pan under the differential. Loosen the fill plug FIRST with a 3/8 hex driver — if it's stuck or stripped, you need to know before you've already drained the axle.
Remove the differential cover bolts in a star pattern. Leave the top two bolts loose to control fluid release.
Crack the cover loose with a flathead screwdriver. Fluid will pour out — let it fully drain (5–10 minutes).
Remove the cover. Inspect the inside of the housing for metal chunks, glitter, or chipped gear teeth.
Wipe the housing interior, ring gear, and magnet (if equipped) clean of old fluid and debris. Reinstall the magnet.
Scrape old RTV from both mating surfaces with a plastic scraper. Wipe with brake cleaner.
Apply a 3/16" bead of RTV around the cover bolt circle, or install a Lubelocker gasket dry.
Reinstall the cover and torque bolts in a star pattern to 30 ft-lbs.
Wait 30 minutes for RTV to set (skip if using Lubelocker).
Pump 75W-90 synthetic gear oil through the fill hole until fluid trickles out the bottom of the fill hole. For Trac-Lok diffs, add 4 oz friction modifier before topping off.
Reinstall and torque the fill plug to 25 ft-lbs. Check for leaks after the first short drive.
pros: Catches metal debris before it grinds the ring and pinion
Cheap insurance — $40 in fluid vs. $1,500+ for a ring-and-pinion replacement
Reveals worn gears, chipped teeth, or excessive backlash early
Synthetic gear oil runs cooler under load
cons: Messy job — fluid drips everywhere if you rush
Requires RTV cure time (or a reusable gasket)
Friction modifier is non-optional with Trac-Lok or it will chatter
The Dana 30 front fill plug is often seized — soak in penetrant the night before

title: Oil Change — 4.0L and 2.5L
tools_required: oil filter wrench (76mm cap or strap)

parts.name: 10W-30 or 5W-30 conventional or synthetic blend (6 quarts 4.0L / 4 quarts 2.5L)

citations.title: AMC/Chrysler 4.0L service manual oil capacity (6 qt with filter)
TJ owner's manual — 10W-30 above 40°F, 5W-30 below

summary: The 4.0L holds 6 quarts of 10W-30 (5W-30 in cold climates) with a spin-on filter. The 2.5L 4-cylinder holds 4 quarts. Drain plug torques to 25 ft-lb, filter hand-tight plus 3/4 turn. Job takes 30 minutes.
description:
The TJ Wrangler runs either the 4.0L straight-six or the 2.5L AMC four-cylinder. Both use a conventional spin-on filter mounted on the lower passenger side of the engine block and a 13mm hex drain plug on the oil pan. The procedures are identical — only the capacity changes.

**Oil viscosity.** The factory called for 10W-30 above 40°F and 5W-30 below 40°F. Either is fine year-round in most climates. Some owners run 10W-40 in hot Southwest summers — the 4.0L wears in for the long haul on anything in this range. Phoenix and Las Vegas owners can safely run 15W-40 conventional. Don't run 0W-20 — the 4.0L has wider bearing clearances than modern engines and will burn it.

**Synthetic or conventional?** Conventional changed every 3,000 miles or full synthetic every 5,000 miles both work. The 4.0L is an old design with loose tolerances; it doesn't reward expensive synthetic the way a modern direct-injected engine does. The exception: if your TJ has 200K+ miles and burns a quart between changes, switching to a high-mileage synthetic blend with seal conditioner can stop leaks at the rear main and valve cover.

**Filter.** Any name-brand spin-on filter that fits the M22x1.5 thread works — WIX 51515, Mopar 5281090, FRAM PH3614, Mobil 1 M1-110A. The filter sits at an angle on the block; expect a quart of mess if you don't position the drain pan right.
steps: Run engine 2–3 minutes to thin oil. Shut off.
Position drain pan under the oil pan plug (rear of pan, 13mm hex).
Remove drain plug. Inspect the gasket — replace if crushed or torn.
While oil drains, reposition the pan under the filter (slightly forward and to the passenger side).
Spin off the old filter (counterclockwise from below). It will dump 4–8 oz of oil straight down — be ready.
Wipe the filter mount clean. Verify the old filter gasket came off with the filter (a stuck gasket is the #1 cause of catastrophic oil leaks after a DIY change).
Wet the new filter's gasket with fresh oil. Spin on by hand until snug, then 3/4 turn more. Do not use a filter wrench to tighten — that's how you crush the can.
Reinstall drain plug with new gasket. Torque to 25 ft-lb.
Add oil through the valve cover fill cap. 4.0L: 6 qt. 2.5L: 4 qt.
Start engine. Verify oil pressure light goes out within 3 seconds. Idle 30 seconds, shut off.
Wait 5 minutes, check dipstick. Top off as needed.
Drive 5 minutes, check for leaks around the filter and drain plug when you stop.
pros: Spin-on filter is the easiest design ever made
30-minute job with hand tools only
Cheap parts at any store
4.0L doesn't care about brand of oil
cons: Filter location dumps oil on the front axle and skid plate every time
Stuck old gasket = oil all over the driveway in 10 miles
Owners who overtighten filters strip the threaded boss in the block (expensive fix)
Drain plug crush gasket is often skipped — leaks slowly until it's noticed

title: Spark Plug Replacement — 4.0L

citations.title: Chrysler TJ 4.0L service info — 0.035" gap, 27 ft-lb plug torque
Champion RC12LYC OEM application data for 4.0L Jeep

summary: The 4.0L takes six plugs, gapped at 0.035", torqued to 27 ft-lb. Copper plugs (Champion RC12LYC or NGK ZFR5N) are the OEM choice and run cleaner than premium platinums on this old engine. Job takes 30–60 minutes with a 5/8" plug socket.
description:
The 4.0L straight-six uses a simple distributor-and-coil ignition through 1997, then coil-on-distributor with cap-and-rotor through 2006. Either way, the plugs sit in a row down the passenger side of the engine, fully exposed, no intake to remove. This is the easiest spark plug job on any modern engine.

**Plug choice.** The factory plug is the Champion RC12LYC copper. NGK ZFR5N is the direct equivalent. Both gap to 0.035" out of the box. Service interval is 30,000 miles on copper, 60,000 on platinum (NGK ZFR5F-11), 100,000 on iridium (NGK IZFR5F-11). On an engine this simple, copper is the better answer: cheaper, runs cooler, easier to read for diagnostics.

**Why not premium plugs?** The 4.0L was designed for copper. Iridium plugs sometimes cause cold-start hesitation on this engine because the precious metal tip has a slightly higher firing voltage requirement and the older ignition coil isn't always up to it. If your TJ runs perfectly on copper and you switch to iridium and get rough idle, that's why.

**Gap matters.** Pre-gapped doesn't mean correctly gapped. Always verify with a wire gauge — 0.035" should slide through with light drag. If you can shove a 0.040" gauge through too, the plug is no good (don't try to close the gap on iridium; the tip chips).

**Anti-seize warning.** Most modern plugs ship with a nickel-coated thread that does not need anti-seize. Adding anti-seize will cause you to overtorque (the lubricant reduces friction, so your torque wrench reads correct but the actual clamp load is too high). If you must use it, a tiny dab on the threads only.
steps: Engine cold (or at least cool to the touch). Hot heads can pull threads out when you remove plugs.
Pop the plug wire boots off one at a time. Twist before pulling to break the seal — don't yank straight up.
Blow compressed air around the plug well to remove any dirt before unscrewing.
Use the 5/8" plug socket with extension. Back the plug out a half turn, then turn by hand the rest of the way to feel for cross-threading.
Inspect the old plug: tan/brown = correct mixture. White/glazed = lean. Black/sooty = rich. Oily = valve seal or piston ring issue.
Check the new plug's gap with a wire gauge. Should be 0.035". Bend the side electrode only, never the center.
Apply a small dab of dielectric grease inside the plug wire boot (helps prevent moisture-related misfires).
Thread the new plug in by hand until snug. If it doesn't go in by hand, stop — you're cross-threading.
Torque to 27 ft-lb with a torque wrench. On an aluminum head this is non-negotiable; the 4.0L iron head is more forgiving but a wrench is still smart.
Reattach the plug wire. Repeat for all six.
Start, listen for misfire. If you have a code reader, scan for P0301–P0306.
pros: Easiest plug job on any modern engine
All six plugs exposed, no intake removal
Copper plugs cost $18 for the set
Old plug condition tells you a lot about engine health
cons: Yanking plug wires straight up tears the terminal off
Hot-engine plug removal pulls aluminum threads out of cylinder heads (rare on 4.0L iron head but possible on 2.5L)
Anti-seize causes overtorque if you don't reduce torque spec by ~25%
Aftermarket plug wires from auction sites cause more misfires than any worn plug

title: Transfer Case Fluid — NP231 and NV231

parts.name: Mopar transfer case fill/drain plug crush washer

citations.title: Novak — Guide to the New Process / New Venture Gear 231 Transfer Case
TJ Forum — Hit 1.5 quarts on 231 transfer case, should I keep going?
TJ Forum — ATF or ATF+4 for transfer case fluid?

summary: The TJ's NP231 transfer case takes about 2 quarts of ATF+4 and the fluid change takes 30 minutes with hand tools — the transfer case is unfussy about ATF brand, but it does need clean fluid every 30,000 miles to keep the planetary gears and chain happy.
description:
The NP231 (later relabeled NV231 after New Venture Gear took over) is the standard TJ transfer case for non-Rubicon builds. It's a chain-driven, part-time 4WD unit with a planetary low range. The lubrication system is simple: ATF splashes from a pump inside the case onto the chain, the planetary, and the bearings. Clean fluid keeps the chain from wearing the case and keeps the bearings from pitting.

Mopar's spec is ATF+4. The forums spend a lot of energy debating whether Dexron/Mercon or other ATFs work — the short answer is yes, they do, the transfer case isn't picky like a modern automatic transmission. ATF+4 is the safe call because it's the manufacturer spec and Walmart sells it for $9 a quart. If you have leftover Valvoline MaxLife from a transmission service, that's fine in the transfer case too.

Capacity is the more useful question. The shop manual says 2.2 pints (about 1.1 quarts), but the real fill range from owners who pump until fluid comes out the fill hole is 1.5 to 2 quarts. The "correct" answer is: pump fluid in until it runs out the fill hole, then stop. Don't trust a fixed number — fluid level varies with how level the rig is parked and where the fill hole is positioned on the case. Park as level as you can manage.

The plugs are both 1/2" drive square plugs — no socket, just stick a 1/2" ratchet directly into the plug. Drain plug is at the bottom of the case; fill plug is on the rear of the case, roughly halfway up. Crack the FILL plug first. If it won't budge, do not drain. A stuck fill plug means you can drain a transfer case you can't refill, and you'll be towing the Jeep instead of driving it.

A common upgrade is a magnetic drain plug — replaces the factory plug, catches metal fuzz, and gives you a diagnostic check at the next service. About $15 from B&M, AFE, or any magnetic-plug vendor.
steps: Park as level as possible. Warm the transfer case by driving a few miles.
Slide a wide drain pan under the t-case.
Crack the FILL plug first (1/2" ratchet drive, rear of case). Confirm it breaks loose. If not, stop.
Remove the drain plug (bottom of case). Let it drain fully — 15–20 minutes.
Inspect the drained fluid. Brown is normal. Milky means water intrusion (check the vent line and any submerged fords). Metal flakes mean internal wear — investigate before refilling.
Reinstall drain plug with crush washer. Torque to 24 ft-lb (snug — these plugs are soft).
Use a fluid pump in the new ATF+4 jug. Pump fluid through the fill hole until it runs out steady. Usually 1.5–2 quarts.
Reinstall fill plug, torque to 24 ft-lb. Wipe down and inspect for leaks after a short drive.
pros: Cheap and fast — 30 minutes, $20 in fluid
No special tools beyond a ratchet
Diagnostic value: fluid condition tells you what's happening inside
Upgrading to a magnetic drain plug catches problems early
cons: Easy to start without confirming the fill plug breaks loose — stuck plug = stranded rig
Manual capacity (1.1 qt) and actual fill (1.5–2 qt) disagree, which causes confusion for first-timers
Plug heads strip if you over-torque — they're soft cast plugs

title: Drag Link Replacement

parts.name: Synergy TJ Heavy Duty Drag Link

citations.title: TJ Wrangler Torque Specs
Wrangler TJ Forum — Tie Rod End Torque

summary: A worn drag link is the most common cause of TJ steering wander and a leading contributor to death wobble — replacement is a one-evening job that restores precise steering feel.
description:
The TJ drag link runs from the pitman arm down to the passenger-side knuckle on the Y-style steering setup that came on every 1997–2006 Wrangler. The tie rod ends are sealed and not greasable from the factory, so they wear out on a predictable schedule — usually around 80,000–120,000 miles, sooner if the truck has been off-road or sees salt. Once the joints develop play, you'll feel the steering wheel wander on the highway, the front end will track over road camber, and bump-steer over uneven pavement will get sharper.

Three replacement paths work depending on your goals. For a stock-tire daily driver, a Moog DS1448 unit is $90–$120 and uses Moog's "problem solver" greasable design that lasts longer than the original. For a lifted truck on 33"–35" tires, the Synergy heavy-duty drag link ($325) gives you a chromoly bar and rebuildable greasable metal-on-metal ends — the same upgrade philosophy as their JK and XJ kits. RuffStuff offers a Y-link conversion that includes a heavier drag link if you're already replacing both the tie rod and drag link together.

If you're going to crossover steering (T-style), the drag link layout changes completely and you'll need a kit designed for that configuration. Don't try to convert with mismatched pieces.

The install is straightforward, but the TJ uses a left-hand thread on the pitman-arm end of some years — check before you start turning anything. Always measure the existing drag link length so you can set the replacement to match and avoid a major alignment swing.
steps: Park level, chock the rear wheels, jack the front axle and put it on stands.
Measure the existing drag link center-to-center between the two TRE centers and write it down.
Remove the cotter pins and castle nuts from both ends. Spec is 55 ft-lb at the TREs and 65 ft-lb at the tie rod / drag link connection.
Use a tie rod separator to pop the ball studs free of the pitman arm and the knuckle.
Note the orientation and thread direction at each end before unthreading the old drag link from any adjusting sleeve.
Thread the new drag link to match the recorded length. Snug clamp bolts lightly until installed.
Install the new drag link in place, install new castle nuts, torque to spec, and continue tightening just enough to align the cotter pin slots.
Install fresh cotter pins. Tighten the clamp bolts to 36 ft-lb (drag link clamp) and 20 ft-lb (tie rod clamp).
Grease the new TREs if they have zerk fittings.
Drop the truck, road test, and get an alignment.
pros: Resolves wander, bump steer, and a major death-wobble contributor
Greasable upgrades last far longer than OEM
One-evening DIY with hand tools
cons: Sealed OEM-style replacements wear again on the same schedule
Some years use a left-hand thread that catches people off guard
Alignment required after install

title: Steering Stabilizer — When It Helps and When It Masks

citations.title: TJ steering stabilizer overview
Why a stabilizer doesn't fix death wobble
Diagnosing death wobble and non-DW shimmies (TJ)

summary: A steering stabilizer is a damper, not a fix — replace yours when it's worn for normal steering smoothness, but if it's the only thing keeping the wheel calm, you have a real problem hiding in your front end.
description:
The TJ steering stabilizer is a horizontal shock that bolts between the axle and the drag link. Its job is to dampen small high-frequency oscillations — tire imbalance, road texture, bump steer over washboard. It is not designed to control death wobble, and a fresh stabilizer that "fixes" a wobble is masking worn track bar bushings, loose tie rod ends, or bad ball joints.

Stock TJ stabilizers wear out around 60,000–100,000 miles. Symptoms of a dead stabilizer: steering wheel kicks sharply over speed bumps, slight shimmy after hitting a pothole, oil leaking down the body of the damper. Replacement is a 30–60 minute job with the right puller.

The Rancho RS5000 RS5407 is the budget pick at around $45 and is the same form factor as the OEM unit. The Bilstein 5100 ($75) gives tighter damping and longer life. Old Man Emu and AEV options run $90–110 and tend to last the longest on a daily-driven TJ. Avoid the cheapest no-name dampers — Rancho has documented issues with internal binding combined with track bar play causing harsh steering feel, and even cheaper units fail faster.

Here's the honest part: if your TJ has shaky steering, you should not replace the stabilizer first. Inspect the track bar bushings (both ends), the tie rod ends, the drag link, and the steering box mount before throwing a new damper at the problem. Jack the front end up and grab the tie rod — any play means a worn end. Grab the track bar at the axle bracket — any side-to-side movement means worn bushings or a cracked bracket. Fix those first. Then replace the stabilizer.
steps: Spray penetrating oil on the stabilizer-to-drag-link stud and the bracket bolt; let it sit 10 minutes.
Loosen the nut on the tapered stud but leave it on by a few threads.
Use a pitman arm puller (rentable free at most parts stores) to break the tapered stud loose from the drag link.
Remove the nut, then unbolt the stabilizer body from the axle bracket.
Install the new stabilizer body to the axle bracket first.
Set the new stabilizer at mid-stroke before tightening the drag link end.
Torque the drag link nut to 35 ft-lbs and install a fresh cotter pin if the nut is castellated.
Bounce the front of the vehicle, turn wheel lock-to-lock, and verify no binding.
pros: Smooths small high-frequency steering inputs
Inexpensive and quick to replace
A fresh unit reduces driver fatigue on washboard
cons: Does not fix death wobble or worn front-end parts
Can mask a serious problem until it fails
Replacing a healthy stabilizer changes nothing about steering accuracy

title: Tie Rod Replacement — Stock and HD Options
tools_required: pickle fork or tie rod separator

parts.name: Moog stock-replacement inner tie rod end (driver)
Moog stock-replacement outer tie rod end (passenger)
RockJock Currectlync HD tie rod kit (TJ/LJ/XJ/MJ/ZJ)
Steer Smarts Yeti XD tie rod

citations.title: Quadratec — RockJock CE-9701 Currectlync HD tie rod kit (84–06 TJ/XJ)
RockJock 4x4 — CE-9701TR Currectlync Tie Rod (Complete)
JeepSpecs — Currie Heavy Duty Steering on the TJ

summary: Stock TJ tie rod ends wear out around 80–120k miles and are a common death-wobble trigger. Replacing them with Moog problem-solver ends ($75–$100 for the pair) restores stock behavior. Heavy-duty kits like the RockJock Currectlync ($600) swap the bent factory rod for a straight 1¼" solid bar — worth it if you run 33"+ tires on rocks, overkill on a daily driver.
description:
The TJ's factory tie rod is a bent steel tube running behind the front axle. Two threaded ends (driver inner, passenger outer) thread into the rod with jam nuts and connect to the steering knuckles via tapered studs. The bent shape was a packaging compromise — it clears the differential but bends easily under impact, and the ends wear at predictable mileage.

**When to replace.** Slop in the tie rod ends shows up as on-center wander, lazy returning-to-center, and at worst, death wobble. Pull the front wheels off the ground, grip each tire at 9 and 3 o'clock, and rock it. Any clunk that doesn't show in the wheel bearing or ball joints is a tie rod end. Visible boot tears mean the joint is contaminated regardless of feel — replace it.

**Stock-replacement vs. heavy-duty.** Moog problem-solver ends (ES3490T driver, ES3491T passenger) install in the existing rod, take about an hour, and bring the truck back to factory feel. About $80 for the pair. For a daily-driver TJ on 31"–33" tires this is the right call.

**The Currectlync upgrade.** The RockJock Currectlync (part CE-9701, fits TJ/LJ/XJ/MJ/ZJ) replaces the rod itself with a 1¼" solid alloy bar — straight, not bent — rated about 200% stronger than stock. It uses 7/8" tie rod ends with included boots. The kit is a direct bolt-in on stock-height to 4"-lifted trucks; over 4" lift you need a 2" dropped pitman arm to keep the drag link geometry correct. Steer Smarts Yeti XD is the other top-tier option, similar concept, slightly different end design.

**Why HD is worth it on a wheeler.** A bent stock tie rod becomes a bent stock tie rod the first time you rock-strike it. A straight 1¼" solid bar takes the same hit and shrugs. If your TJ sees real rocks, the upgrade pays for itself the first time you avoid trailering home.

**Set toe correctly.** Whatever rod you install, set toe before the alignment shop sees it. Target 1/16" to 1/8" toe-in with the wheels straight ahead. Measure between tire tread centers at the front and rear of the tire — the front measurement should be 1/16" to 1/8" smaller. Loosen jam nuts, twist the rod to adjust, retighten to 55 ft-lb. Then take it for an alignment to confirm camber and caster.
steps: Park on level concrete. Loosen front lug nuts. Lift the front and set on jack stands. Pull both front wheels.
Diagnose — rock each tire 9/3, look for clunk independent of wheel bearing.
With ignition on and helper turning the wheel, watch each tie rod end joint for independent movement.
Measure existing toe between tire centers, front and rear of tire, to know where to set the new rod.
Loosen jam nuts at each end of the tie rod. Note approximate thread engagement.
Remove cotter pins and castle nuts at the knuckle. Use a tie rod separator (not a pickle fork — pickle fork damages the boot of any part you intend to reuse).
Unthread the rod from both ends or pull the entire assembly and transfer to new HD kit.
Install new ends or new HD rod. Snug to length matching the original measurement.
Set toe to 1/16"–1/8" toe-in.
Torque castle nuts (40 ft-lb, then tighten to align cotter pin slot — never back off). Install new cotter pins.
Torque jam nuts to 55 ft-lb.
Road test. Then alignment shop within a week.
pros: Restores precise steering feel
Eliminates a common death-wobble trigger
HD kit takes rock impacts that bend stock
Bolt-in with hand tools
cons: HD kit is $600+
Over 4" lift requires a dropped pitman arm to keep drag-link geometry
Pickle fork removal damages boots — use a proper separator
Always follow with an alignment to nail camber and caster

title: Track Bar Replacement — TJ Specifics

parts.name: Synergy TJ/LJ adjustable front track bar
Currie RockJock Johnny Joint adjustable track bar
Rough Country adjustable front track bar

citations.title: Synergy TJ Adjustable Front Track Bar
RockJock TJ Trac Bars
TJ Front Track Bar Torque

summary: The TJ front track bar locates your axle side-to-side; if you've added a lift over 2" or you feel highway wander, replace it with an adjustable HD bar to re-center the axle and stop death wobble.
description:
The TJ front track bar uses a tapered-stud mount on the frame side and a bolt-through bracket on the axle side. The factory bar is fine at stock height, but when you lift the front the axle shifts toward the driver side because the bar pulls it that way through the lift arc. After a 2"–4" lift, an adjustable bar is required if you want the steering to feel right.

The TJ has one quirk worth knowing: the factory frame-side mount uses a tapered hole. Some aftermarket bars (Synergy, RockJock) keep the tapered fitment; others (cheaper bars) convert it to a straight through-bolt and require drilling the axle bracket to 9/16". The drilled-out conversion is permanent. If you want to keep the option of reverting to a stock bar, choose a bar that preserves the taper.

Brand picks: Synergy 8520-01 ($360) — dual-durometer bushings, Teflon bearing, maintenance-free, quiet ride. RockJock CE-9120TJJ ($330) — 4130 chromoly tube with rebuildable Johnny Joints, the choice for hard wheeling. Rough Country adjustable ($160) — budget option, urethane bushings, fine for daily-driver lifts under 3". For stock-height TJs replacing a worn factory bar, OEM Mopar 52088433AB ($145) is a direct swap.

Symptoms that you need a new track bar: steering wheel off-center on a straight road, axle visibly off-center between the wheel wells, clunking over bumps from worn bushings, or active death wobble after hitting a bump at 45+ mph. Death wobble has multiple causes (worn ball joints, loose tie rod, bent steering link), but a worn track bar is the single most common trigger.

Final torque happens at ride height. The factory spec is 74 ft-lbs at the frame side and 55 ft-lbs at the axle bracket — these are lower than JK numbers because the TJ uses smaller hardware. Aftermarket bars with larger bolts will specify their own torque, often 100–125 ft-lbs. Always follow the bar manufacturer's torque spec for the supplied hardware.
steps: Park on level ground, set parking brake, chock rear wheels.
Loosen front lug nuts, lift front, set on jack stands under frame, remove wheels.
Measure frame rail to inner tire edge on both sides — record.
Support front axle on floor jack to take tension off the track bar.
Remove the axle-side bolt first (typically 18mm head).
Remove the frame-side bolt (21mm) — note tapered stud fitment if applicable.
Compare new bar to old at equal length as starting point.
Install frame side first, then axle side, finger-tight.
Reinstall wheels, lower to ride height.
Torque to manufacturer spec at ride height.
Re-measure axle centering — adjust bar length if off by more than 1/8".
Drive 50 miles, re-check all torque.
pros: Cures TJ death wobble from worn factory bar
Adjustable bar re-centers axle after lift
HD bars resist bending on rocks
Bolt-in install if you choose a bar that keeps the tapered mount
cons: Some bars require drilling the axle bracket — irreversible
Tapered-stud mount can seize and be hard to remove
Torque-at-ride-height step is critical or bushings wear early
Bar replacement alone won't fix death wobble if ball joints or tie rod are also worn

title: TJ Front Coil Spring Replacement

parts.name: Old Man Emu front coil 2" lift (heavy)

citations.title: Steps for replacing front coil springs — TJ Forum
2003 Jeep TJ Torque Specifications — Wandering Trail
Stock Spring Swap Walk-Thru — TJ Forum

summary: Front TJ coils come out the top of the spring perch once you drop the axle and disconnect the track bar — no spring compressor needed for stock or up to 3.5" coils.
description:
The TJ uses a coil-sprung four-link front suspension that descends directly from the XJ, but with shorter coil pockets and a panhard (track) bar that has to come loose before the axle can drop far enough to free the springs. Almost every TJ coil swap turns into a half-hour fight at the track bar because the bolt is captured in a tight bracket and the bushing is corroded onto the sleeve. Spray it with penetrant the night before and the job goes faster.

Pricing splits cleanly: OEM Mopar coils are around $100–$120 each, used to refresh a sagging stock rig. Aftermarket 2"–3" lift coils run $200–$350 a pair. Old Man Emu 2937 heavy-rate fronts are the daily-driver favorite for owners running a winch or steel front bumper; Currie and Rubicon Express are the mid-tier choices; Rock Krawler and Clayton sit above $400 with progressive-wound springs. For 4"+ lifts you'd be doing this swap as part of a full kit with longer shocks and adjustable control arms.

The TJ's geometry gets touchy past 3.5" because the factory control arms are short and the panhard angle steepens as the axle drops. Going beyond 3" of coil lift without adjustable arms will leave the axle pulled to the passenger side and the caster down around 1°–2° (factory spec is 7°). You'll feel the wandering on the freeway before you make it home from the install. Either keep the lift at 3" or budget for adjustable control arms and a longer or adjustable track bar in the same project.

Drop the axle slowly. The coils are captive in the lower spring pocket by a retainer clip but the upper pocket is just an isolator. Once the axle drops about 5 inches the coil tension is gone and the spring will sit loose in the pocket. Don't let it fall out and bend the lower isolator. After install, the bumpstops should sit roughly 1" off the axle pad with the rig on the ground — if they're touching, the coils are sagging or the wrong rate. If there's a 3"+ gap, you may need bumpstop extensions to prevent the shock bottoming out before the bumpstop does.

Torque specs that matter on this job: front shock at axle 21 ft-lb (this is correct, not a typo — it's a small bolt), spring retainer clip 16 ft-lb, sway bar end link 75 ft-lb, track bar at frame 40 ft-lb, track bar at axle 125 ft-lb, lower control arm at axle 130 ft-lb, lower control arm at frame 115 ft-lb.
steps: Loosen front lug nuts. Spray track bar bolt and sway bar end link bolt with penetrant.
Lift the front of the Jeep, support on stands under the frame just behind the front axle.
Remove front wheels. Place a floor jack under the differential.
Disconnect one sway bar end link at the axle (18mm, T55). One side is enough — keeps the axle from twisting.
Disconnect the track bar at the axle bracket (21mm).
Unbolt both front shocks at the axle (13mm long bolt, 10mm box end on shaft).
Slowly lower the floor jack to drop the axle.
Once coils lose tension (~5" of drop), remove the spring retainer clip at the lower seat (13mm).
Tilt the coil and pull it out the top.
Install the new coil — seat it in the upper isolator and lower spring pad.
Reinstall the retainer clip (16 ft-lb).
Jack the axle back up, reconnect shocks, track bar, sway bar end link. Snug only.
Lower the Jeep to the ground.
Final-torque: shocks 21 ft-lb, track bar 125 ft-lb at axle and 40 ft-lb at frame, sway bar end link 75 ft-lb.
Get an alignment. Caster target: 5°–7°.
pros: Stock or 3"-or-less coils swap with no spring compressor
Bolt-in with hand tools
Wide aftermarket — heavy-rate fronts available for built-up rigs
Doesn't require pulling brake lines
cons: Track bar bolt is the bottleneck — penetrant the night before
3.5"+ lifts pull caster out of spec; need adjustable arms
Bumpstop height after install needs to be checked
Always get an alignment after — caster shift is unavoidable

title: TJ Lift Kit Options — Coil vs. Long Arm

parts.name: Rough Country 2.5" budget boost coil spacer kit
Old Man Emu 2.5" coil and shock kit
Rubicon Express 3.5" Super-Flex short arm kit
Clayton Off Road long arm upgrade kit (4.5")

citations.title: Choosing the Right Jeep Lift Kit: Long vs. Short Arm Lift Kits
Long arm vs adjustable short arm worth the $$$?
Metalcloak TJ Long Travel Short Arm Lift Kit

summary: Up to 3.5 inches of lift on a TJ, stay with a short arm kit and adjustable arms — it's cheaper, bolts in, and rides fine. At 4 inches and beyond, the stock control arm angles get steep enough that a long arm upgrade is worth the welding and the money.
description:
The TJ runs a coil-sprung suspension at all four corners, which makes lift kits cleaner than the leaf-sprung XJ. The catch is the short factory control arms: when you lift the body, the axle pivots forward through an arc, caster drops, and the driveshaft angles steepen. Coil spacers ignore all of that and just push the body up. New taller coils with matched shocks address ride height correctly. Adjustable control arms fix axle position and caster. Long arms fix the geometry by moving the control arm pivot rearward, which flattens the arm angle and brings the suspension closer to factory geometry at full lift height.

Tiers worth knowing about: a budget coil spacer kit from Rough Country runs about $250 and gives 2 to 2.5 inches — fine for a daily driver clearing 31s, terrible if you want to actually flex on a trail. A mid-range new-coil kit (Old Man Emu Heavy 2.5", Rubicon Express Super-Flex 3.5", Metalcloak Game-Changer 3.5") sits in the $1,200 to $1,800 range with shocks and adjustable arms — this is the sweet spot for the vast majority of TJ builds. A long arm upgrade from Clayton, Savvy, or Currie runs $2,500 to $3,500 plus install, requires welding new frame brackets onto the unibody, and only makes sense if you're building for 35-inch tires, 4.5+ inches of lift, or daily rock crawling. Rough Country's long arm kits are cheaper but cut corners on bushings and brackets — many TJ owners report squeaks and premature wear.

The single most important add-on at any lift height is the slip yoke eliminator (SYE) plus a CV rear driveshaft. At 3 inches and up, the stock NP231 transfer case output is at an angle the slip yoke can't handle, and you get vibration that no amount of u-joint cycling will fix. Budget another $700 to $1,000 for the SYE and driveshaft on top of the lift itself. A 3.5-inch short arm kit, slip yoke eliminator, adjustable track bars, and an alignment is the most common "complete" mid-range TJ build.

Don't lift higher than you need. Each inch of lift pushes the center of gravity up, hurts on-road manners, and forces another bracket of compromises (adjustable track bar, longer brake lines, longer sway bar end links, possibly re-gearing). A 3-inch TJ on 33s is a more capable trail rig than a 6-inch TJ on 35s for most people.
steps: Decide tire size first. Lift exists to clear the tires you want — not the other way around.
Pick a lift height: 2 to 2.5" clears 31s and 32s, 3 to 3.5" clears 33s, 4"+ for 35s.
At 3" and up, plan for: adjustable track bars (or relocation brackets), SYE and CV rear driveshaft, longer brake lines, longer sway bar links.
Pick coil spring rates appropriate to your weight — front winch bumper and rear tire carrier require heavy springs.
Install kit per manufacturer instructions. Torque all suspension bolts at ride height, not at droop.
Get a four-wheel alignment after install. Caster should land between 4 and 6 degrees.
Re-check torque after the first 100 miles on the trail.
pros: Coil suspension means lifts are usually bolt-in up to 3.5"
Mid-range short arm kits give 95% of the long arm benefit at half the cost
TJ aftermarket support is deep — every brand makes a kit
Adjustable arms recover caster without welding
cons: Cheap coil spacer kits ride harshly and don't add wheel travel
Long arm kits require welding and frame fabrication
Any lift over 3" needs SYE plus CV driveshaft, adding $700–$1,000
Lift adds rollover risk if you stack lift on lift on tires

title: Rear Leaf Spring Replacement

parts.name: Old Man Emu CS049R Medium Load Rear Leaf (TJ)
Rubicon Express Standard Coil Rear Lift (TJ uses coils, not leaves — note: TJ is coil-rear)
Rancho RS44113 TJ Rear Leaf (NOTE: TJ rear is coil — see body)

citations.title: Old Man Emu YJ Rear Leaf CS036R reference
Wrangler Forum — TJ vs YJ leaf spring discussion

summary: The TJ is a coil-sprung Wrangler — if you're searching for a TJ "rear leaf spring," you've either got an LJ-to-leaf conversion build, or you're confusing the TJ with the older YJ Wrangler. This guide covers both situations.
description:
Stock TJ Wranglers (1997-2006) and LJ Unlimiteds (2004-2006) use coil springs front and rear — not leaves. That's the headline. If you came into the garage expecting leaf-spring perches under the rear axle, you've got a YJ (1987-1995) or an aftermarket leaf-conversion kit. The coil-sprung rear is one of the TJ's biggest advantages over the YJ: better articulation, smoother ride, easier to lift.

That said, there are two real reasons to land on this page. First: you own a TJ with an aftermarket leaf-spring conversion (rare, usually shop-built for racing or specific suspension geometry). Second: you're cross-shopping a TJ with a YJ build and want to understand the differences. The TJ's coil-and-track-bar geometry is covered in detail in our [TJ Coil Spring Replacement guide](tj/suspension/coil-spring-tj.md). If your goal is rear lift, you want coil springs, not leaves.

For the rare TJ-with-leaves build (typically a Currie or shop-built setup): leaf packs are sized by load rating and arch. Old Man Emu, BDS, and Skyjacker make spec-matched leaves for YJ that physically bolt to a TJ-to-leaf conversion frame bracket — but you need to confirm bushing eye diameter and arch height against your specific conversion kit. Mopar OE leaves do not exist for the TJ because the platform was never coil-rear from the factory.

Replacement procedure (for the conversion build): support the frame, remove the U-bolts holding the axle to the spring pack, swing the spring forward off the front eye bolt, remove the rear shackle, replace the spring pack with the new one, torque U-bolts to 90-100 ft-lb in a cross pattern. Re-torque after 500 miles — leaf packs settle.

If you bought a TJ and want a 2-3" rear lift, you're shopping coil springs. Skip this guide and go to the coil spring page.
steps: Confirm your TJ actually has leaf springs in the rear (look for a multi-leaf pack between axle and frame). Stock TJ = coils, not leaves.
If coil-rear: stop. Go to the TJ coil spring guide.
If leaf-converted: chock front wheels; lift the rear; support frame on jack stands behind the axle.
Place a floor jack under the axle for support.
Spray penetrant on U-bolt nuts; let sit 10 minutes.
Loosen and remove U-bolt nuts; remove U-bolt plate and U-bolts.
Loosen the front eye bolt and rear shackle bolts.
Lower the axle to relieve tension on the spring pack.
Swing the spring forward off the front eye; remove the shackle; pull the spring out.
Install the new spring: front eye onto front mount bolt first, then rear into the shackle.
Center the axle on the spring perch (use the center pin alignment hole).
Reinstall U-bolts and plate; torque to 90-100 ft-lb in a cross pattern.
Torque front eye bolt to 80 ft-lb; shackle bolts to 55 ft-lb.
Drive 500 miles; re-torque U-bolts.
pros: Cheaper than coil-and-track-bar replacement (for conversion builds)
Leaf packs are tough and tolerant of bad geometry
Easy to add load capacity by adding leaves
cons: TJ was not designed for leaves — converting from coils gives up articulation
Confusing platform mismatch: most TJ owners actually want the coil guide
Aftermarket conversion brackets are not common; parts harder to source
Rides stiffer than coil-rear unless tuned with proper shocks

parts.name: Prothane front control arm bushing kit (poly)

summary: Worn control arm bushings cause vague steering, clunks over bumps, and uneven tire wear; replacement requires pressing the old sleeves out — most TJ owners replace the whole arm instead of fighting the press job.
description:
The TJ has eight control arm bushings — two per arm at each end, four arms total. They wear by 80,000-150,000 miles depending on use, and a lifted TJ that's seen mud or saltwater destroys them faster. Symptoms: clunking on direction changes, steering wander, premature inner-edge tire wear, and a "loose" feel that doesn't track straight on the highway. Grab each arm and try to twist it — significant rotational play at the bushing eye means it's done.

Three real options:

**Replace the bushings in your existing arms.** Cheapest at $60-$80 in parts, but the labor is the catch. The bushing sleeves are pressed into the arm eye and bonded with rubber. Burning the rubber out with a torch, drilling the sleeve, and cutting it with a sawzall is the proven method — a 12-ton shop press will handle the new bushing install. Plan four to six hours total. Poly bushings (Prothane 1-204, Energy 2.3106) transmit more road noise than rubber but last twice as long.

**Replace the whole arms with new OE-spec ones.** Replacement arms with fresh bushings run $35-$50 each in stamped steel from MOOG or Dorman. Total: $140-200 for all four, no press work needed. This is the right call for most owners.

**Upgrade to tubular arms with rebuildable joints.** Currie, Clayton, and JKS make tubular arms with Johnny Joints or similar — $280-$500 per pair. Rebuildable for life, much stronger than stock stamped arms, and necessary above a 3" lift to correct geometry.

Whatever you choose: torque to spec **with the suspension at ride height**, not with the wheels hanging. Torquing at full droop preloads the bushings and tears them apart within a year.
steps: Park on level ground. Loosen the lug nuts before jacking.
Lift the front, set on jack stands under the frame. Support the axle with a floor jack so it stays at ride height.
Soak control arm bolts with penetrating oil. These are 18mm and notoriously rusty.
Remove the lower arm first — one bolt at the frame, one at the axle bracket. Repeat for the upper.

If pressing bushings: burn out rubber with a torch (in open air, away from fuel lines), drill the sleeve, slot it with a sawzall, collapse it inward, drive out. Press new bushings in with a shop press.
If swapping whole arms: install new arm, hand-thread both bolts.
Repeat for remaining arms. Switch to the rear and repeat — same process, different arm geometry.
Lower the vehicle so the suspension is at ride height. Torque all control arm bolts to 130 ft-lb.
Test drive at low speed checking for clunks. Get an alignment within 100 miles.
pros: Restores tight steering and bump feel
Stops premature tire wear
Replacing whole arms avoids the press job entirely
Poly bushings last twice as long as rubber
cons: Pressing bushings is genuinely difficult — most owners pay a shop $100-150 per arm
Poly bushings transmit road noise
Must torque at ride height or you'll destroy the new bushings
Alignment required after
